fridayMoons.reseated: The second and third moons are not out today. The ship falls back into orbit around {body}.

nibiru.noteFar: A world with no sun, falling in out of the dark on a course nobody plotted and nobody can bend. The ephemerides put it over Earth on the twenty-first of December, 2012.
nibiru.noteNear: Inside the system now, and no longer slowing. It holds Earth's own angle exactly, which is another way of saying it is not going to miss.
nibiru.saturnNote: Nibiru went into the giant instead, and the giant caught. Saturn burns now: not enough to be a star, far too much to still be a planet. The rings went first.
nibiru.towerNote: Where Earth stood there is a black lance twelve kilometres tall, gold at every edge, turning in the orbit its world left behind. Nothing on it answers, and one door is open.
nibiru.entered: Nibiru has crossed into the Solar System.
nibiru.hitSaturn: Nibiru has struck Saturn. The giant is burning.
nibiru.hitEarth: Nibiru has struck the Earth. Both are gone.

DF-224 Computer.label: DF-224 Computer
DF-224 Computer.note: The onboard computer. 48 kilobytes, three redundant processors, one left.

Thermal Blanket.label: Thermal Blanket
Thermal Blanket.note: Multi-layer insulation, cracked and peeling after a decade of raw sunlight.

Aperture Door.label: Aperture Door
Aperture Door.note: Shuts if the Sun comes within 20 degrees of the axis. It has stuck before.

High-Gain Antenna.label: High-Gain Antenna
High-Gain Antenna.note: The downlink. Everything the telescope has ever seen came through here.

Battery Bank.label: Battery Bank
Battery Bank.note: Six nickel-hydrogen batteries carrying the night side of every orbit.

Solar Array (Starboard).label: Solar Array (Starboard)
Solar Array (Starboard).note: Its twin. Same fault, opposite side.

Solar Array (Port).label: Solar Array (Port)
Solar Array (Port).note: Twenty-five square metres of cells. Warps every time it crosses the terminator.

Reaction Wheels.label: Reaction Wheels
Reaction Wheels.note: Four wheels that turn the whole observatory by turning themselves.

Gyroscope Assembly.label: Gyroscope Assembly
Gyroscope Assembly.note: Six rate gyros, three needed to point. They fail on a schedule.

Fine Guidance Sensor.label: Fine Guidance Sensor
Fine Guidance Sensor.note: Locks onto guide stars. Without it the telescope cannot hold still.

NICMOS Cooler.label: NICMOS Cooler
NICMOS Cooler.note: Keeps the infrared detectors at 60 K. The solid nitrogen ran out.

STIS Spectrograph.label: STIS Spectrograph
STIS Spectrograph.note: Splits starlight into its lines. Power supply is marginal.

WFPC2 Camera.label: WFPC2 Camera
WFPC2 Camera.note: Wide field and planetary camera. The one that takes the pictures.

Corrective Optics (COSTAR).label: Corrective Optics (COSTAR)
Corrective Optics (COSTAR).note: The spectacles fitted in 1993 to undo the mirror's error.

Secondary Mirror.label: Secondary Mirror
Secondary Mirror.note: Holds the focus. Micrometeoroid pitting across the coating.

Primary Mirror.label: Primary Mirror
Primary Mirror.note: 2.4 m, ground to the wrong prescription in 1981. Spherical aberration.

hubbleQuest.title: Refit of the Hubble Space Telescope
hubbleQuest.body: The old observatory is still up there, holding its one astronomical unit orbit and pointing at nothing. Half its assemblies are dead, the rest are running on their margins, and the downlink has been quiet for years. Bring the ship alongside, open the servicing bay and put the telescope back to work one assembly at a time.
hubbleQuest.objectives: Restore every assembly of the Hubble Space Telescope from the ship's servicing bay.
terms: The bay only opens while the ship holds station in the telescope's orbit, in the Sol system.
Every repair is paid for in crafting materials, and a worse fault costs more.
Nothing here is timed: a half-serviced telescope stays half-serviced.
hubbleQuest.reward: Deep field imaging: double range on the biosignature sweep

bodyNote.2060chiron: Comet or asteroid, depending which year you ask. It grew a coma in 1988, after a decade filed as a minor planet, and the argument has not been settled since.
bodyNote.3753cruithne: Earth's second moon, if you are generous. A horseshoe co-orbital that takes 770 years to walk one lap of its bean-shaped path around us, and is never captured.
bodyNote.433eros: NEAR Shoemaker touched down here on 12 February 2001, a spacecraft never designed to land on anything. It kept transmitting from the surface for a fortnight.
bodyNote.antichthon: Philolaus placed a Counter-Earth opposite our own, forever behind the Sun, to round the count of moving bodies up to ten. Every probe sent to check has been aimed somewhere else.
bodyNote.earth: The shell around it is not decoration. Forty years of spent upper stages, dead satellites and frozen coolant, every collision breeding the fragments for the next one.
bodyNote.hubblespacetelescope: Launched 1990 with a primary mirror ground to the wrong prescription by two microns. Three servicing missions have been flown to it. It needs a fourth.
bodyNote.moon2: The second moon keeps a five day week. It is up there on a Friday, full and unhurried, and on every other day the sky where it should be is empty. No ephemeris in print admits it.
bodyNote.moon3: The third rises with the second and sets with it, further out and smaller, and has never been photographed on a Thursday. The two of them are always in the same phase as each other and never in the Moon's.
bodyNote.pioneer10: Launched 1972. It keeps falling short of where the arithmetic says it should be, by a hair, every year. Carries a gold plaque of two naked strangers waving.
bodyNote.pioneer11: Launched 1973, first to Saturn. Last contact 30 November 1995: the transmitter is dead, the trajectory is exact, and the plaque aboard is still legible to nobody.
bodyNote.russellsteapot: China, elliptical orbit between Earth and Mars, too small for the most powerful telescope to confirm. The burden of proof is not on the observer. Confirmed.
bodyNote.titania: One ocean, all of it acid, wrapped around a hole four hundred thousand times the Sun. The Dargos live on the water and refer to the hole as the neighbour. Humanity has had a standing invitation here since 1977 and nobody on Titania has yet stopped finding that funny.
bodyNote.tma2: A black slab in Jupiter space, its edges in the exact ratio 1:4:9 to the limit of measurement. Every instrument aimed at it returns the reflectance of nothing at all.
bodyNote.voyager1: The furthest human object from the Sun, returning 160 bits a second from the edge of the heliosphere. The Golden Record is bolted to its flank, never once played.
bodyNote.voyager2: Launched 1977, the only craft to pass all four giants. Its plasma instrument is still switched on. Nobody at the Deep Space Network has ever had a reason to switch it off.
bodyNote.vulcan: The planet Le Verrier put inside Mercury's orbit in 1859 to explain the wandering of Mercury's perihelion. General relativity explained it instead. Vulcan was never withdrawn, only stopped being looked for.
